analysis.investment_thesis: Bandhan Bank is a microfinance-rooted bank undergoing a painful transformation, operating in a segment where asset quality can deteriorate violently during economic stress — as FY22's near-zero profit of ₹126 Cr illustrated. With ROE of only 11.2%, no identifiable deposit franchise moat, and finance costs growing at a 26.6% CAGR (faster than revenues), I see no compelling reason to own this over better-run Indian private banks.
key_strengths: Impressive earnings recovery: net profit rose from ₹126 Cr (FY22) to ₹2,745 Cr (FY25) as MFI stress normalized
Total debt declining sharply (₹24,711 Cr → ₹11,138 Cr over 3 years), improving the liability structure
Forward P/E of 10.9x and P/B of 1.14x mean the stock is not pricing in a rosy scenario
key_risks: Microfinance credit cycles are brutal: FY22 showed profits can collapse from ₹2,000 Cr+ to ₹126 Cr in one year; this can repeat given India's rural borrower stress
Finance costs rising at 26.6% CAGR vs revenue CAGR of 7.8% — the cost of liabilities is growing far faster than earning assets, compressing spreads
Promoter at 39.7% (Bandhan Life Insurance) creates ownership complexity; RBI has historically flagged promoter concentration issues with this bank
red_flags: OCF was −₹4,245 Cr in FY23, reflecting the extreme volatility of a bank with heavy MFI concentration — banks with this profile are fundamentally difficult to analyze
ROE of 11.2% is below my 15% minimum threshold — a bank this risky should be delivering materially higher returns to justify the complexity
I do not understand the MFI credit cycle well enough to predict when the next stress event occurs; the geography of Bandhan's borrowers (eastern India, Bengal) concentrates political and flood risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Banking is a business I approach very carefully — I want the best-run bank at a fair price, not a recovering bank at a cheap price. Bandhan started as a microfinance institution and converted to a bank in 2015. Its historical strength was deep distribution in underbanked eastern India, but that same geographic concentration and borrower profile creates acute credit risk. FY22 demonstrated this: the COVID aftermath nearly wiped out profits entirely (₹126 Cr on a ₹138,995 Cr asset base). The recovery since is commendable, but the ROE still sits at 11.2% — not exceptional for the risk taken.

The forward P/E of 10.9x implies the market expects earnings to roughly double from FY25 levels. That may or may not materialize, but I am not the right person to bet on MFI credit cycles normalizing. Finance costs have risen 26.6% annually for three years, squeezing spreads as rates rose. The bank is pivoting toward home loans and secured credit, which is sensible but takes years to meaningfully shift the portfolio. I prefer to watch from the sidelines.
